repos.title: Turns Matter: Advancing Streaming Video RL via Turn-Level Credit
repos.paper_summary:
TurnWise is a turn-level GRPO framework for streaming video RL that gives each response-or-wait decision its own advantage and weights decisions equally in the loss. For each trajectory, it scores every prefix with all later turns set to silence, subtracts the reward accrued before each turn, and normalizes the remaining return within the rollout group. Turn-mean aggregation averages token losses within each turn, then across turns, so output length does not set a turn's weight. No critic or extra rollouts are needed.

On Qwen2.5-VL-3B, TurnWise reaches 43.56 PAUC on ProactiveVQA, 21.59 Timing F1 on OVO-Timing, and 49.43 average accuracy on StreamingBench, which are 3.96, 3.87, and 0.69 points above the strongest non-TurnWise results. On Qwen3-VL-4B it reports 42.44, 11.15, and 58.96. Adding turn-mean aggregation to turn-level credit cuts repetition from 15.53 to 5.98 relative to credit-only training.

Limitations: experiments cover two Qwen backbones and three benchmarks, and the reward is the fixed PAUC-based scorer from MMDuet2. The alpha sweep tests only four correction strengths.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Shared trajectory-level advantages misassign credit to redundant replies and useful follow-ups in streaming video reinforcement learning.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior streaming video methods use trajectory-level GRPO, which broadcasts one advantage across all decision turns.

digest_headlines.heading: Methodology
digest_headlines.headline: Silence-completed prefix scores give each turn a remaining-return advantage, and turn-mean averaging weights every turn equally.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Experiments compare TurnWise with fine-tuned and reinforcement-learning baselines on three streaming benchmarks using two Qwen backbones.

digest_headlines.heading: Results and Discussions
digest_headlines.headline: TurnWise posts the best aggregate scores on all three benchmarks, reaching 43.56 on ProactiveVQA with the 3B backbone.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Turn-level credit without a critic supports higher-quality, better-timed and more selective streaming responses.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix derives the telescoping decomposition, the group-relative correction, the interpolation and warm-up schedule, and the dual-clipping loss.

repos.title: TSFLab: A Self-Improving Agent-Agnostic Workbench for Time Series Forecasting Research
repos.paper_summary: TSFLab is an agent-agnostic workbench that gives coding agents shared time series forecasting (TSF) resources: a domain guide, a structured catalog of 323 integrated models and 93 datasets with 71 reusable units, a unified experiment runner, and a verification loop that folds verified additions back into the shared workbench. The workbench is evaluated with Codex CLI and GPT-6 Luna on three tasks: reproducing four recent papers (12 attempts), benchmarking eight methods on two new datasets (48 results), and a method-development pilot on ETTh1 and Weather. Against TSLib, TFB, and no workbench, TSFLab completes 12/12 reproductions and 42/48 benchmark results, the most of any setting. Its completion rate is 20–163% higher and fresh tokens per completed task are 11–66% lower across baselines. In reproduction, 73% of 96 scheduled results fall within 10% of the paper's MSE, versus 21–46% for other settings. The method-development pilot reports 32.8–73.6% fewer fresh tokens and 9.2–68.8% less time, but produced no new method that substantially outperforms leading forecasters. Results come from one agent family and a single run configuration, and the paper states that the workbench is untested outside forecasting.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Only about one in five of 1,707 papers since 2020 provides code, so agents face outdated knowledge and inconsistent settings.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior libraries, agent systems and workbenches lack shared TSF evaluation protocols, and self-improving agents improve only a single agent.

digest_headlines.heading: TSFLab
digest_headlines.headline: TSFLab gives any compatible agent four modules: domain guidance, structured knowledge, a unified experiment runner, and verified shared updates.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: TSFLab completes the most tasks, 12/12 reproductions and 42/48 benchmark results, against 8/12 and 26/48 without a workbench.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: TSFLab improves completion and token efficiency and supports method development without changing agents, and it retains verified results for later agents.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitations
digest_headlines.headline: Results cover only forecasting tasks, and method development has not yet produced a method that substantially outperforms leading models.

digest_headlines.heading: Ethical Considerations
digest_headlines.headline: Coding agents should run sandboxed with explicit authorization for external actions, and results should be read under recorded protocols.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists the 17 skills, knowledge card examples, command and budget details, datasets, fixed protocols, metric definitions and price assumptions.

repos.title: Axion 1.0: Open Agent Foundation Models, Simplified
repos.paper_summary: Axion 1.0 is an open agent foundation model trained in three stages: two supervised fine-tuning (SFT) stages, then reinforcement learning (RL), with no mid-training, DPO, or on-policy distillation. Stage I trains on science problems generated from public seeds and made harder using the base model's own solutions. Stage II trains on tool-use questions built by deterministic filter, select, and compute programs over structured databases that are hidden during solving. RL uses GRPO with partial credit for verified intermediate steps. The authors release data construction code, prompts, and training code. On full Humanity's Last Exam (HLE) with website access restricted, the 35B and 122B models score 52.2% and 59.0%. Against Agents-A1 (47.6%), the 35B model is 4.6 points higher on HLE, 5.8 points higher on SEAL-0, and 7.0 points higher on FrontierScience Olympiad. The 122B model reaches 66.7% on FrontierScience Research, above GPT-5.6 Sol's 63.3%, but scores 41.7% on BioMysteryBench, below GPT-5.6 Sol's 47.1%. Limitations: each score is the best of one run, baselines come from mixed sources and tool settings, and the stage-contribution results in Section 4.3 are cut off in the provided text.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Axion 1.0 asks whether a three-stage recipe without dedicated mid-training, direct preference optimization or on-policy distillation can still yield broad agentic capabilities.

digest_headlines.heading: Data Construction
digest_headlines.headline: Both data pipelines build questions with verified reference answers and keep only correctly solved trajectories for training.

digest_headlines.heading: Training
digest_headlines.headline: Training runs two supervised stages then reinforcement learning, with partial credit for verified intermediate steps.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: Under restricted web access the 122B model scores 59.0% on Humanity's Last Exam and 66.7% on FrontierScience Research.

digest_headlines.heading: Training Infrastructure
digest_headlines.headline: Separate infrastructure trains long 128K-token trajectories with sharding and runs asynchronous reinforcement learning with token-consistent rollouts.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Axion differs from related agent, data and training-consistency work by using a simpler two-stage supervised sequence followed by reinforcement learning.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The authors conclude that simpler, data-centric pipelines can produce strong agent models, with code and data released.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists supervised and reinforcement learning hyperparameters and three case studies comparing checkpoints across training stages.

repos.title: History Forcing: Distilling History-Dependent Continuations for Long-Horizon Video World Models
repos.paper_summary: History Forcing is a distillation framework for few-step autoregressive video diffusion models that adds a history-dependent correction to the distillation target. For each student chunk, a frozen autoregressive teacher predicts the same noisy chunk with and without extra history. The difference between the two scores, scaled by a weight $\lambda$, is added to the reference score in distribution matching distillation, or to the teacher velocity target in on-policy self-distillation. For long-video generation, the history comes from earlier student chunks. For out-of-sight world modeling, it comes from a fixed-camera teacher rollout. On 15s VBench generation, the variant with a 10s-fine-tuned teacher scores 85.07 quality, versus 84.44 for the baseline without history supervision. On 60s VBench-Long, a 1.3B student reaches an aggregate score of 79.82, above Rolling Forcing (79.22) and LongLive (79.12) and below the 5B LongLive-2.0 (79.90). On the PlayWorld Out-of-sight subset, Evolution Quality rises from 2.35 to 2.70. On MemoBench Real, Object Consistency rises from 58.43 to 62.18. Limitations: long-video experiments use only 1.3B models, world-model experiments use one 5B backbone, and gains are bounded by how well the teacher models temporal dynamics.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: History Forcing adds a history-based correction to distillation so long video rollouts keep subjects and scenes consistent.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work adds history through memory or training changes, but leaves the contribution of history implicit in distillation targets.

digest_headlines.heading: Preliminaries
digest_headlines.headline: Background defines flow-matching velocity, chunk-wise autoregressive factorization, and distribution matching distillation gradients.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: History Forcing adds a history-contrast residual to the reference score for long videos and to velocity targets for revisits.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: History Forcing scores highest among 1.3B students on VBench-Long and improves out-of-sight revisit metrics on both benchmarks.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: History Forcing reduces drift in long videos and keeps object states across out-of-sight gaps, within limits set by the base models.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists training, inference and evaluation settings and additional qualitative examples for both applications.

repos.title: The Trinity:Capability-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Multimodal Agents
repos.paper_summary:
The Trinity is a recursive self-improvement framework that evolves the agent Harness, the wrapper around a frozen multimodal backbone, by grouping tasks according to shared capability requirements rather than surface categories. Evolver derives requirements from verified trajectories and builds a capability tree from the task tree. Creator builds simplified, verifiable training worlds for each node, and Explorer evolves reusable modules along a Harness tree. A Capability-Aware Harness Router selects a compatible branch for each new task using public task information and stored feedback.

The paper reports that evolved Harnesses improve mean performance by 34 points across 28 training benchmarks and by 26 points across 18 unseen benchmarks, including two real-world embodied tasks. The training/unseen split is fixed before capability induction, and unseen tasks are excluded from tree construction and routing memory, so the unseen result measures transfer.

The authors note two limitations: retrieval coverage and result quality for web-search benchmark discovery vary across queries, and the study centers on Harness-level self-improvement rather than training model parameters.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Manual Harness iteration and costly environment construction limit multimodal agents, so The Trinity evolves Harnesses along shared capability requirements.

digest_headlines.heading: Preliminaries
digest_headlines.headline: Long-horizon multimodal tasks depend on a Harness of six control protocols that coordinate a frozen model.

digest_headlines.heading: The Trinity
digest_headlines.headline: The Trinity builds a capability tree from training trajectories and evolves Harness modules in verified simulated worlds.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Across 28 training and 18 unseen benchmarks, mean Train score rises from 39.1 to 73.2 by Iteration 4.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work covers harness self-improvement and agent–environment co-evolution, where Trinity induces a capability tree from trajectories.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Capability-driven self-improvement with capability-aware routing improves aggregate performance and transfers to two real-world embodied settings.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: The stated limitations are web-search benchmark discovery and a focus on Harness-level self-improvement only.

digest_headlines.heading: Authors
digest_headlines.headline: The author section lists core contributors, contributors, three corresponding authors, and nine affiliations.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix describes the task tree, capability and Harness trees, evaluation details, and per-benchmark decision figures.

repos.title: VisSearch-Bench: Evaluating Long Horizon Visual Search in Multimodal Agents
repos.paper_summary: VisSearch-Bench is a benchmark of 204 human-written tasks for evaluating visual context management in long-horizon open-web search by multimodal agents. The tasks span five categories: Set-wise Visual Search, Sequential Visual Search, Hybrid Wide–Deep Search, Competitive Visual Disambiguation, and Visual-Structure-Guided Search, across 7 primary and 25 secondary domains. Annotators build each task from public sources with a reference answer and traceable evidence, and automated checks plus human review remove tasks that can be solved without the visual evidence. Accuracy requires the predicted answer to contain all and only the required content. Process Score is the fraction of labeled critical states recovered, averaged over tasks. Across 16 models and agent setups, the best system reaches 26.47% accuracy, a ReAct agent with Kimi-K3. Direct answering by GPT-5.5 scores 6.37%, and ReAct with GPT-5.5 reaches 25.49%. Several open-source models score 0.00% accuracy on the direct setting. The paper states that the benchmark's 204 tasks are a limited sample and that the construction relies on human annotation.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Some search tasks use images only to identify an entity, so the paper tests how agents link visual evidence across steps.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: VisSearch-Bench is the only listed benchmark that covers set answers, evidence links, and partial credit together.

digest_headlines.heading: VisSearch-Bench
digest_headlines.headline: Each of 204 tasks is built from public sources with traceable evidence, a locked answer, and human review.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Search lifts accuracy well above direct answering, but the best system still fully solves only 26.47% of tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Verifying multiple objects and combining findings into consistent answers remain open challenges for multimodal search agents.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists related benchmark details, prompts, hyperparameters, release fields, and seventeen case-study trajectories.

repos.title: AnyGameRenderer: Entity-Consistent Generative Rendering Across Games and an Entity-Level Benchmark
repos.paper_summary: AnyGameRenderer is a video-to-video generative renderer that restyles crude game footage, such as gray blockouts, colored primitives, semantic maps, and wireframes, into finished visuals while keeping each entity's position, timing, and count. It is a LoRA (rank 128) fine-tune of the MiniMax-H3 ref2va model, a 33B reference-video-conditioned generator, trained on 10,330 paired clips from three sources: 3,221 clips of multi-stream renders from 38 GEAR games, 3,910 clips of two-stream Unreal Engine scenes with scripted crowds and count changes, and 3,199 clips of real recordings converted to crude 3D-box inputs. A structured six-segment caption states which crude shape stands for which entity and what must be preserved. The authors also propose an entity-level benchmark of 59 cases with 753 entities, scored with temporal match, position match, unrendered rate, and hallucination rate. Against the zero-shot base, temporal match rises from 50.9% to 62.9%, missed count changes fall from 34.7% to 21.3%, and hallucination falls from 52.1% to 46.0%. Gains are smallest on real recordings (46.5% to 51.1% temporal match). The benchmark relies on SAM3 detection and tracking, so scores depend on that pipeline.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Crude game footage can be re-rendered in a chosen style while keeping every entity's count, position and timing.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Earlier systems rely on fixed intermediate representations, and none measures entity-level correspondence.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: A rank-128 LoRA on MiniMax-H3 is trained with a six-segment caption that fixes which crude shapes are entities.

digest_headlines.heading: Data
digest_headlines.headline: Training pairs come from 38 agent-made games, scripted Unreal Engine scenes and real recordings, totaling 10,330 clips.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: On 59 held-out cases, temporal match rises from 50.9% to 62.9% and missed count changes fall from 34.7% to 21.3%.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The renderer keeps entities in sync across genres and crude input types, with gains shown on one held-out benchmark.

repos.title: PhotoGuider: Composition-Aware Cropping and 360$^{\circ}$ View Framing with Explainable Photographic Assessments
repos.paper_summary: PhotoGuider is a method for choosing a viewing direction in a 360° panorama and framing a photo within it, using four interpretable photographic tokens (Subject, Composition, Integrity, Aesthetics) computed from pretrained vision models. Compact LightGBM rankers and gates, with about 63k parameters, select and refine crops. A fine-tuned MLLM explainer, distilled from Qwen2.5-VL-7B, produces explanations conditioned on the token measurements. On FCDB and FLMS, the paper reports an average mIoU of 0.811 for the full mode against 0.792 for Venus and 0.789 for Cropper, with average BDE of 0.044. Fine-tuning reduced the explainer's measured contradiction rate from 6.31% to 1.55%. In a 120-participant blind ranking of 100 Poly Haven panoramas, framings were ranked first 53.2% of the time, against 27.3% and 19.5% for two alternatives. Limitations stated by the authors: refinement uses discrete step fractions, and view selection returns a single argmax without user control.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Panoramic framing needs a direction choice before cropping, which PhotoGuider addresses with four interpretable photographic tokens.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior croppers, critics, and view selectors offer scores that are hard to inspect or check against measurements.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: PhotoGuider ranks shortlisted candidate framings with four photographic tokens, then refines the top frame with gated moves.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: PhotoGuider's full mode scores highest average mIoU, 0.811, on two 2D benchmarks and places first in 53.2% of 360° rankings.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The authors list discrete refinement steps and a single view argmax as limitations.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists token feature definitions, candidate sources, gate details, consultant and explainer settings, and user study analyses.

repos.title: RESPLE2: Inertial-Informed Recursive Non-Uniform Spline Estimation for Multi-Sensor Odometry with Global Refinement
repos.paper_summary:
RESPLE2 is a recursive multi-sensor odometry framework that represents 6-DoF motion as a non-uniform B-spline and estimates it with an iterated extended Kalman filter. When a knot is added, its control point is predicted from a subset of IMU measurements using the knot-clamping property of B-splines, and a reset step corrects control points over the new knot spacing. The update step fuses LiDAR, camera, IMU, and leg-kinematic measurements at their native timestamps. Knots are placed adaptively from IMU-derived changes in position, orientation, and velocity. A global module refines control points using loop closures detected with iBTC.

In a HOPPER ablation, IMU-informed prediction reduces position APE (RMSE) relative to a constant-transition-matrix baseline by about 39% to 76%, with the largest reduction on high1, from 0.017 m to 0.004 m. On flip1, RESPLE2 uses 2087 control points versus 2362 for Coco-LIC, 11.6% fewer. Per-LiDAR-frame runtime is 15.4%, 18.3%, and 10.6% of the time budget on flip1, `day_open`, and Outdoor1. The abstract claims "competitive or superior" accuracy against other multi-sensor odometry systems, but the main comparison tables are not in the provided text, and the ablations use only HOPPER sequences.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Existing multi-sensor odometry is sensor-specific, and uniform B-spline estimators cannot predict control points from inertial data.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior B-spline systems either predict control points without exact kinematics or lack native loop-closure refinement.

digest_headlines.heading: Preliminaries
digest_headlines.headline: Cubic non-uniform B-splines and their kinematics define the recursive state of the four most recent control points.

digest_headlines.heading: System Overview
digest_headlines.headline: RESPLE2 predicts each new control point from inertial samples, resets the spline, then runs an iterated update.

digest_headlines.heading: Generalized Spline State-Space Modeling with Multi-Sensor Measurements
digest_headlines.headline: Clamping each new knot lets the control point be predicted exactly from inertial measurements.

digest_headlines.heading: Inertial-Informed Iterated Extended Kalman Filter on Non-Uniform B-Splines
digest_headlines.headline: The iterated extended Kalman filter propagates an augmented 33-dimensional state over inertial substeps, then updates.

digest_headlines.heading: Global Refinement
digest_headlines.headline: Loop-closure constraints refine all control points by least squares while odometry residuals keep adjacent control points consistent.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: On every handheld sequence, RESPLE2 has at least one variant with the lowest odometry error.

digest_headlines.heading: Further Discussions
digest_headlines.headline: Inertial-informed prediction lowers position error on all legged-quadcopter sequences, and knots concentrate near ground impacts.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Reported accuracy matches or exceeds baselines in real time, with visual constraints independent of LiDAR depth left as future work.

repos.title: RoboScope Kit: Unified Interfaces for Fast and Scalable Embodied-AI Evaluation
repos.paper_summary: RoboScope Kit is a shared evaluation layer for robot-policy benchmarks. Each model is wrapped once as a Policy class, and each benchmark is wrapped once as an adapter around its native evaluator, so benchmark rules and scoring stay unchanged. A scheduler runs simulator workers and Policy replicas as separate pools, sizes both with a time-bounded concurrency search over short probes, and shards work deterministically across GPU instances. Runtime optimization renders only the observations a chunked Policy reads. Adapters cover six benchmark families. On LIBERO-Long with a StarVLA checkpoint on one RTX 4090, the search selects twelve workers and three replicas, which evaluate 500 episodes 4.45× faster than the official StarVLA evaluator, with equivalent success rates. With CUDA MPS, sixteen workers and four replicas give 6.16× speedup. On RoboTwin Easy, four GPUs with chunk-boundary observation finish 500 episodes in 14.4 minutes, 25.04× faster than the single-GPU baseline, with identical success outcomes and terminal steps. The speedups are measured against the official evaluators and the baselines named in the paper, and the evidence covers two benchmarks in detail. Search time adds 506 s on LIBERO-Long.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: RoboScope Kit wraps models and benchmarks once and separates simulator workers from model replicas to speed evaluation.

digest_headlines.heading: Background and Motivation
digest_headlines.headline: The official StarVLA evaluator leaves the GPU at 14.3% average utilization because simulation and per-step handling dominate CPU time.

digest_headlines.heading: Design
digest_headlines.headline: The design separates simulator workers from Policy replicas and uses a diagonal search to size both from measured probes.

digest_headlines.heading: Implementation
digest_headlines.headline: The implementation packages a Python Policy API, native benchmark evaluators, and a six-family adapter catalog that run as separate local processes.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: RoboScope Kit matches official LIBERO-Long outcomes and evaluates 4.45 times faster than StarVLA, and 6.16 times faster with CUDA MPS.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: The related work places the paper among evaluation harnesses and simulation engines that separate simulators from inference.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Search cost is large on short workloads, so reporting search time beside evaluation time shows when automation pays off.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The system matches official outcomes and cuts evaluation time 4.45 to 6.16 times on LIBERO-Long, and 359.7 to 14.4 minutes on RoboTwin Easy.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists Policy lifecycle methods, benchmark contracts, work-queue states, experimental details, tuning runs, and adapter catalog.
